subject: english-language
title: Idioms and Oxymorons
welcome_lead: Some phrases mean more than they say. Crack the code.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on idioms, oxymorons and figurative twists.
final_note: You can now decode idioms and notice oxymorons.

concepts.def: Joke using a word's double meaning.

walkthroughs.body_html: 'Spill the beans' has nothing to do with beans — it means 'reveal a secret'. Idioms only make sense to insiders.
Oxymoron: short phrase joining opposites ('bittersweet'). Paradox: longer idea that seems impossible but reveals truth.
A pun plays on multiple meanings. A cliché is an idiom worn out by overuse — avoid in your own writing.

mcqs.q: Are claims that women use more 'tentative' language well-supported?
options: Women always use more hedges and tag questions than men.
Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
Early studies (Lakoff) made broad claims, but later research (e.g. Holmes, Cameron) shows context matters more than gender, and many supposed differences disappear with proper data.
Women and men have different vocal cords so speak differently.

mcqs.q: What does Labov's research show about language variation?
options: Labov showed that working-class people speak ungrammatically.
Women and men have different vocal cords so speak differently.
Language varies systematically by social class, gender, age and context — and speakers shift style depending on formality, often unconsciously.
Labov showed that everyone speaks the same way regardless of background.

mcqs.q: Is language change a sign of decline?
options: Language change shows that standards are falling and English is being ruined.
No — modern linguistics treats change as natural and continuous, not as decay. Every language has always been changing and will continue to.
Language change only happens in informal speech, not in writing.
Labov showed that everyone speaks the same way regardless of background.
